paras: The lynching of Van Canady was the hanging of a young Black man, also called John Carson, by a crowd that took him from the jail at Shelby, North Carolina, just after midnight on December 1-2, 1888. Canady had been accused of murdering James Philbeck, a white farmer, and was reported to have confessed the day before. A coroner's jury found that he died "at the hands of parties unknown", and the story ran as a brief across the country, while North Carolina papers called the lynching just punishment.

On the night of November 21 or 22, Philbeck, a farmer of about 60 living near Shelby in Cleveland County, was called to his door and shot dead; his wife was shot and the house robbed. Canady, described as a "mulatto" of about 22 or 23 from Iredell County, was arrested on suspicion; a Shelby dispatch put the arrest on Sunday, November 25, while the Raleigh wire said he was arrested on Saturday, December 1.

According to a Charlotte special of December 1, the sheriff traced Canady to the murder after arresting him for three burglaries, and Canady confessed, naming his brother Charlie Armstrong as having helped him. At the coroner's inquest on Philbeck that day, the sheriff presented the written confession rather than the prisoner "for fear he would be lynched", and the jury named Canady guilty and Armstrong an accessory. The dispatches reported "great excitement" and fears of a lynching, and an extra guard was put on the jail.

Just after midnight on Saturday, a crowd gathered near Shelby, on horseback and on foot, and chose a leader. The Charlotte dispatch called it "an orderly crowd of about 100 persons" made up of whites and Blacks, the Raleigh wire said two hundred masked and armed men, and a Shelby dispatch said about 200, "many not being disguised." The crowd overpowered or surprised the guard; the Raleigh wire said a "stout negro" who took part broke open the jail door; the cell locks were broken, by one account with a sledge-hammer.

The lynchers put a rope around Canady's neck and led him about a mile east of town, where they threw the rope over the limb of an oak. He was given time to confess and pray, and the papers reported that he called his sentence just. He was then tied on a horse, which was driven or pulled from under him.

The body hung until the afternoon or evening, about five hours by one count, when the coroner had it taken down. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of "Died of strangulation at the hands of parties unknown." No arrests of the lynchers, grand jury action, or later proceedings against Armstrong appear in the coverage.

The story spread in two main forms: a Raleigh wire, headlined "Lynch Law in North Carolina" in New Haven and run in Savannah and Alexandria, and a Charlotte dispatch printed in the New York Sun under "A Negro Murderer Taken from Jail by a Mixed Mob and Hanged." Briefs stressing the confession, such as the Sacramento item headed "Said He Deserved I[t]", ran on December 3-5 in Sacramento, Washington, Augusta and Annapolis, and weekly digests carried the story into mid-December in North Dakota, Rhode Island and West Virginia.

Southern papers framed it more openly: the Savannah Morning News headlined "Tar Heel Lynchers Avenge the Murder of the Philbecks," and a Kentucky weekly's head read "His Confession Was Evidence Sufficient." The Charlotte Democrat called Canady a "negro brute" and "human fiend" whose dying was "the agony so justly due for his dastardly deed," and the Progressive Farmer called him a "disreputable mulatto." The Durham Recorder printed his reported words that his punishment was "merited, just and an honor to the country."

The size of the crowd varied with the source: about 100 in the Charlotte dispatch, about 200 in the Raleigh wire and the Shelby dispatch, and twenty mounted men in the Progressive Farmer. Most reports put the lynching about midnight on December 1-2, but one weekly digest gave "the 1st" and the Progressive Farmer "the night of the 3rd"; the Shelby and Charlotte dispatches of December 2 and 3 are closest to the event.

accounts.label: Raleigh wire (Dec. 3)
accounts.gist: Two hundred masked and armed men overpowered an extra guard near morning; a 'stout negro' broke open the door; the prisoner was taken a mile from Shelby and swung from the back of a horse.

accounts.label: Charlotte/Shelby dispatch (Dec. 3)
accounts.gist: An orderly crowd of about 100 whites and blacks chose a leader, broke two locks, led Canady a mile east and hanged him from an oak after he prayed and called his sentence just; a coroner's jury found death at the hands of parties unknown.

accounts.label: Shelby dispatch (Dec. 2)
accounts.gist: About 200 men met a mile west of town, broke the cell locks with a sledge-hammer about midnight, many undisguised; the guard was surprised and offered no resistance; the body hung until evening.

accounts.label: Progressive Farmer (N.C. weekly)
accounts.gist: Twenty mounted men rode in on the night of the 3rd, the jailer refused the keys, and the body hung about five hours before the coroner had it lowered.

framing.detail: The Charlotte Democrat called Canady a 'negro brute' and 'human fiend' whose death throes were 'the agony so justly due for his dastardly deed'.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Swung from a Horse. Tar Heel Lynchers Avenge the Murder of the Philbecks', and the Big Sandy News 'His Confession Was Evidence Sufficient'.
The Progressive Farmer had called the unknown killer 'the monster' and then described Canady as a 'disreputable mulatto' while reporting the lynching flatly.
Northern and western papers carried short briefs under heads such as 'Lynch Law in North Carolina' and 'Said He Deserved I[t]', stressing the confession.
